## 2. Geoff's Pork Belly Thai Basil

Geoff's version of a Thai basil stir-fry, taken down over the phone. Pork belly and chicken in a screaming-hot wok, sauced by feel, finished with Thai basil and the green tops of scallions, served over rice.

**Whose is whose, since 2026-09-12.** **The dish is Geoff's** — the wok sequence, the meat-before-aromatics order, the sauce order and the seasoning are all his and none of it has been touched. **What changed is one thing: how the pork belly gets cooked before it hits the wok.** Geoff simmers it; **Cody cooks it sous vide now**, and that is his own revision, made after cooking the dish and deciding the boiled belly tasted boiled. **Geoff's simmer is kept in full as [§2.D, the variation at the end of this entry](2-geoffs-pork-belly-thai-basil.md#d-variation--geoffs-original-simmer)** — his words, his 45–60 minutes, his warning about going too soft — and it is still the right answer on a night when you don't have a day and a half.

**The texture history, because it is the whole reason the revision exists.** There are **two failure modes in this dish and they sit on opposite sides of the same step.** The belly started out **chewy** — that was the original problem, and Geoff's simmer was the fix for it. Cody cooked it that way and the simmer overshot into the other ditch: ***"it just tasted a little boiled. The pork belly tasted boiled a little bit when I boiled it, because I think I boiled it too long."*** So the sous vide has to do **both** jobs — break the belly down the way the simmer did, without the boiled flavor. **A bath that leaves the belly chewy has failed the revision even if nothing tastes boiled.** That is why the default below is a long bath at a moderate temperature rather than a short hot one: Cody's own reasoning, and it is correct — ***"sometimes the length of the sous vide, the length of how long you sous vide a meat, can soften it up — soften up the collagens over time."*** Collagen converts to gelatin as a function of time as much as temperature, and at moderate temperatures time is the lever.

**Two things worth knowing before you start.** First, the pork belly is cooked, cooled and cut **before** the wok is ever lit — that is now a two-day head start, not an hour, so read the countdown and start early. Second, once the wok is hot this whole dish runs in about ten minutes and there is no time to go chop something. Everything gets prepped and lined up within arm's reach first. Geoff's own words: expect it to take two cooks to nail the timing, and by the second one you won't need the recipe.

**Techniques used:** [T2 Hot Pan First, Then Oil](t2-hot-pan-first-then-oil.md) · [T27 Sous Vide "Not-So-Premium" Cuts](t27-sous-vide-not-so-premium-steak-cuts-codys-method.md) · [T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization — GBD](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md)

**🟡 Medium** · **Prep ~35 min** *(5 min to season and bag the belly two days out; ~30 min on the day — cubing the cold belly, then chopping and lining everything up)* · **Cook ~15 min** *(the wok, start to finish, and none of it is unattended)* · **Slow cook 36 hr** *(sous vide, unattended)* · **Start to finish ~2 days** *(36 hr in the bath, then at least 4 hr — better overnight — chilling before the belly can be cut and seared)*

**⏰ Countdown to dinner:** T−2 days season the pork belly — kosher salt, garlic powder, black pepper only — bag it dry, into the bath at 155°F for 36 hr · T−12 hr belly out of the bath, straight into an ice bath 20–30 min, then into the fridge overnight *(4 hr is the floor)* · T−45 min cube the cold belly and pat the cubes bone dry · T−40 min chop and line up absolutely everything — nothing gets chopped once the wok is hot · T−15 min wok ripping hot, oil, belly cubes in 2–3 min undisturbed for the sear marks, then out onto a plate · T−12 min chicken 5–7 min, aromatics and chili, vegetables 2 min, sauces in order, belly back in with the sauce, palm sugar, umami and white pepper, chili and sesame oil, basil and green tops 30 sec–1 min · T−0 over jasmine rice, rice stays out of the wok.

**❤️ Family favorite** — *Cody: "Love it."*

> ♨️ **The sous vide numbers are cookbook judgment, not Cody's — [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md), and flagged here where you will see it.** **His are the decision and the reasons:** sous vide instead of boiling, *"a little bit softer,"* the wok finish with sear marks, and the instruction that the bath must run long enough to soften the collagen. ***"Use your judgment with how long you're supposed to sous vide pork belly, and use your judgment with what temperature you're supposed to sous vide pork belly."*** **Every number below — 155°F, 36 hours, the chill, the sear seconds — is the cookbook's**, reasoned from the published sources named in the callout under Step 2. **His own figures supersede these the day he gives them**, and he has already said he intends to find out: *"let's just see what it tastes like."*

> 🧊 **The bag stays plain, and that is deliberate on a Thai-seasoned dish.** Per [CLAUDE.md §6](../../CLAUDE.md) and [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md)'s established rule, a sous vide bag in this house is **kosher salt, garlic powder and black pepper only — no fresh garlic, no liquid.** Fresh garlic sealed in a bag at sub-boiling temperature is an anaerobic botulism setup; garlic powder is the safe substitute. [§T27](t27-sous-vide-not-so-premium-steak-cuts-codys-method.md) and [§T28](t28-sous-vide-chicken-codys-method.md) both carry it forward. **No soy, no fish sauce, no basil, no chili goes in that bag** — every bit of the flavor in this dish arrives in the wok, in Geoff's order, in the last ten minutes. The bath is a texture step, nothing else.

### A. Ingredients

**Meat**

- 1–1.5 lb pork belly, left whole for the bath (sliced is fine if that's what you have — it just chills and cubes differently)
- 1–1.5 lb chicken, cut into bite-size pieces

**For the pork belly bag** *(dry only — see the bag rule above)*

- Kosher salt
- Garlic powder — **not** fresh garlic
- Black pepper

**Aromatics & vegetables**

- 1 yellow onion, chopped
- 4–6 cloves garlic, chopped
- 1 bunch green onions — whites and greens separated, both sliced
- 2–3 cups frozen mixed vegetables, thawed (eyeball it)
- 1 large bunch Thai basil or holy basil, leaves picked

**Heat — pick one**

- 1 tsp Thai chili sauce (spoon out the solids), **or**
- 1–2 tsp Chinese chili oil, added at the very end instead

**Sauces & seasoning**

- Vegetable oil or peanut oil, 2–3 Tbsp (**not** olive oil — smoke point is too low)
- Soy sauce — one full pass over the surface of the wok
- Dark soy sauce — half the amount of the soy sauce
- Oyster sauce — a quarter to a half the amount of the soy sauce
- Fish sauce — about the same as the soy sauce, maybe a touch less
- 1–2 Tbsp palm sugar, grated
- Umami seasoning blend (Trader Joe's) — a light sprinkle over the whole surface
- White pepper — about the same amount as the umami; 1–2 Tbsp total for both. Black pepper works in a pinch
- 1–2 tsp sesame oil, at the end

**To serve**

- Jasmine rice, cooked, served separately

**Equipment worth having:** a **sous vide circulator** and a **vacuum sealer or zip-top freezer bags** (water-displacement method if you're not sealing), a wok, and two squirt bottles (the yellow-and-red mustard-and-ketchup kind, not trigger sprayers) — one for soy sauce, one for fish sauce. The squirt bottles are not required, but it's how the hibachi cooks hit fried rice with soy, and it makes the fast part of this dish much easier.

### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. Two days out: season the pork belly and bag it. About 5 minutes.**
Leave the belly whole. Kosher salt, garlic powder and black pepper on all faces — **that is the entire bag**, per the rule above. Vacuum seal it, or use a zip-top freezer bag and the water-displacement method to press the air out. Nothing wet goes in, and no fresh garlic goes in. **Do not do any of this to the chicken** — the chicken is cooked fresh in the wok and would fall apart on you.

**2. Sous vide at 155°F for 36 hours.**
**This is the step that replaces Geoff's simmer, and it is doing the simmer's job — breaking the belly down so it doesn't eat chewy.** Bag in the water, lid or a covered pot to slow evaporation on a bath this long, and walk away; nothing about these 36 hours can go wrong. **Why so long:** collagen converts to gelatin over time as much as with temperature, so a long hold at a moderate temperature breaks down far more connective tissue than a short one at a higher temperature — which is exactly the softening Cody asked for. It comes out fully cooked, tender through, and still firm enough to hold an edge when you cut it. *(Same shape of cook as [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md)'s chuck, which runs 36 hours as the house standard — in the bath one evening, out the next. The lead time is already this kitchen's rhythm.)*

> 🔬 **Where 155°F/36 hr comes from, and the two other ways to run it.** *Cookbook judgment per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md) — the sources are named, the pick and its reasoning are the cookbook's, and **Cody's own figures supersede them the day he gives them.***
>
> | Run it this way | Source | What you get |
> |---|---|---|
> | **155°F for 36 hr** — **the house default** | **J. Kenji López-Alt, *Serious Eats*** (his all-belly porchetta) | Fully broken down but still **meaty and sliceable** — holds a clean edge, which is what takes a sear mark |
> | **158°F for 16 hr** — the overnight version | **ChefSteps** | Genuinely tender, holds its shape — but **20 fewer hours of collagen conversion**, so this is the one most likely to still read chewy |
> | **168–170°F for 10–11 hr** — the fast one | **Anova's** published pork belly recipes | The softest, in a **braise-like, nearly falling-apart** way — and it gives up the sear, because it won't hold an edge in a wok |
>
> **Why the long one wins here.** Chewiness is the problem being solved, and time at a moderate temperature is what solves it — **36 hours at 155°F does far more collagen conversion than 16 at 158°F**, and three degrees is noise beside twenty extra hours. It is also **the one of the three built for exactly this finish**: Kenji's 155°F belly is meant to be chilled, cut and then hit with violent high heat — he deep-fries it — and a belly that survives deep-frying will hold its edge in a wok and take the marks Cody asked for. **Higher and faster is the wrong trade.** At 168–170°F the belly goes soft the *other* way: the muscle squeezes out moisture and turns shreddy, which eats soft but falls apart the moment it's tossed, and there are no sear marks on something that won't hold an edge. **Reach for the 16-hour bath when you genuinely don't have a day and a half** — it is a real option and it is better than boiling — but know that it's the one that risks reproducing the chewiness this revision exists to fix.

**3. Chill the belly hard before you cut it. Ice bath 20–30 minutes, then the fridge — overnight is best, 4 hours is the floor.**
**Do not skip this and do not cut it warm.** Straight out of a 155°F bath the belly is soft and will tear, smear and fall apart under a knife; chilled all the way through it cubes cleanly and then *sears* instead of collapsing in the wok. **This cookbook makes this exact argument twice already and it isn't restated here — go read it**: [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md) Step 13 on why *you physically cannot slice 130°F beef paper-thin*, and [§6.10 Sous Vide Brisket](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md)'s overnight ice-chest day, which is the same move at brisket scale. Bag unopened into ice water first — ice pulls it down fast and evenly where a fridge works slowly from the outside in — then the fridge. *(The 20–30 minutes and the 4-hour floor are the cookbook's numbers, reasoned from those two entries.)*

**4. Cube the cold belly and pat the cubes bone dry.**
Out of the bag, onto the board, **bite-size cubes** — the size you'd want on a fork with a piece of chicken. Then **dry them**, every face, with paper towels. **A wet surface steams and greys instead of searing**; that is [§T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md), and it is the same reason [§T2 Hot Pan First, Then Oil](t2-hot-pan-first-then-oil.md) is in this recipe's technique line. Don't restate it — know it. Save the juice in the bag if you want it; a spoonful goes into the wok fine with the sauces, but it is not part of the recipe.

**5. Prep absolutely everything else.**
Chop the garlic and the onion. Take the green onions and split them: the **white parts** go in early with the garlic and onion, the **green tops** go in at the very end. Pick your basil leaves. Get the mixed vegetables out of the freezer so they're fully thawed. Cut the chicken. Set your sauces out and open. Once the wok is hot this dish moves fast, and you want to be reaching for things, not looking for them.

**6. Get the wok ripping hot, then add the oil.**
Full blast. As hot as your burner goes, and leave it there for the entire cook. Watch the dry wok until you see a wisp of smoke come off it — that's your signal it's ready. *Then* pour in the vegetable oil and swirl it around the sides. **Don't walk away at this point.** Hot oil in a dry wok is the one place in this recipe where you can start a fire. Have the pork belly right there and add it within a few seconds.

**7. Sear the pork belly cubes first. 2–3 minutes, mostly undisturbed — then out of the wok onto a plate.**
**The belly goes in alone and it comes back out.** Lay the cold, dry cubes into the swirled oil in one layer and **leave them alone** — that is how you get the marks Cody asked for; a cube you keep flipping never sits still long enough to brown. Give the first face a couple of minutes, turn them once, another minute, and **get them onto a plate.** They are already fully cooked; you are buying color and nothing else. *(The 2–3 minutes is the cookbook's figure, not Cody's or Geoff's; go by the color of the crust.)* ⚠️ **The belly renders hard here** — if the wok is swimming, pour some off before the chicken goes in, or the sauce won't cling later.

**8. Brown the chicken. About 5–7 minutes.**
Chicken into the same wok and the same fat. The water coming out of it immediately takes the fire risk off the table. You're not looking for fully cooked yet, just browned — you'll know it when you see it. **This is the step that used to hold both meats; now it holds only the chicken**, and the reason is in the callout below.

> ⚙️ **The split-and-reunite sequence in Steps 7, 8 and 12 is the cookbook's reasoning — not Geoff's and not Cody's — and it is in Open Questions for Cody to confirm the first time he cooks it this way.** **The problem it solves:** in Geoff's original, the belly and the chicken went into the wok together for 5–7 minutes because both were raw-ish. **They are no longer in the same state.** The belly comes out of the bath already cooked and already broken down; the chicken is raw. The minutes the raw chicken needs would cook a done belly past done, and a belly that has given up its collagen **will break apart over seven minutes of tossing** — you would lose both the sear marks and the cubes. **So each protein is cooked on its own and they are reunited at the saucing stage**, which is ordinary wok practice for exactly this reason. **Nothing else in Geoff's sequence moved**: meat still goes in before the aromatics, the sauces still go in his order, the fond still gets scraped, the smell is still the timer, the basil is still last, and the rice still stays out of the wok.

**9. At about three-quarters browned, add the aromatics and the chili.**
Garlic, chopped onion, the white parts of the green onion, and about 1 tsp of Thai chili sauce all go in now. *This is Geoff's deviation from every video and every Cajun cook you'll hear from* — they all start the garlic, onion, and peppers first. He puts the meat in first on purpose, because aromatics that go in at the start of a full-blast wok cook come out burnt and bitter by the end. Scoop the chili sauce with a spoon so you're pulling out the solids; a little of the liquid coming with it is fine.

**10. As soon as you smell the garlic and onion, add the mixed vegetables. Cook 2 minutes.**
That smell is the timer — not the clock. Add the thawed mixed vegetables and stir everything up really well.

**11. Sauce it, in this exact order, moving quickly.**
Heat stays on full blast the whole time.

- **Soy sauce first.** One pass over the entire surface of the wok — like a hibachi cook hitting fried rice. Everything should look moist; you're not trying to saturate or pool it.
- **Dark soy sauce next**, about half the amount of the soy sauce.
- **Oyster sauce**, a quarter to a half of the soy amount. You almost can't use too much of this. The only thing to be careful of is burning it.
- **Fish sauce last**, roughly the same as the soy sauce — maybe a touch less, but no need to cut it in half.

Give it a quick stir so nothing sits and scorches, and **scrape the bottom of the wok** the same way you'd scrape a Cajun pot. The fond stuck to the metal is flavor; leave it there and you've thrown it away.

**12. The pork belly goes back in, right here with the sauce.**
Everything on the plate from Step 7 back into the wok, and **fold it through rather than tossing it hard.** This is the moment it glazes: the sauce is on the metal, the sugar hasn't gone in yet, and from here it's only about two minutes to the finish — long enough for the belly to come back to temperature and take the sauce, short enough that the cubes stay cubes and the sear you bought in Step 7 is still there on the plate.

**13. Grate 1–2 Tbsp palm sugar right over the top.**
Straight over the wok on a grater. It'll melt into the sauce as you stir.

**14. Season with umami blend and white pepper.**
A light sprinkle of the Trader Joe's umami seasoning across the whole surface, then about the same amount of white pepper — 1–2 Tbsp total between the two, at the most. Black pepper is a fine substitute for the white if you're out. *The umami blend is the one item worth a special trip: it's a Trader Joe's product, and Geoff struck out looking for it anywhere else. White pepper is on the shelf at any grocery store.*

**15. Chili oil and sesame oil go in near the end. Don't cook them long.**
If you're using the Chinese chili oil instead of the Thai chili sauce, this is where it goes in — 1–2 tsp. Same for the sesame oil. Both of these lose what makes them good if you cook them; they go in seconds before the basil, essentially at the same time.

**16. Add the Thai basil and the green onion tops. 30 seconds to 1 minute — watch it, don't time it.**
Both go in together. All you're doing is softening the leaves. This is an eyeball step: the second the basil wilts and goes glossy, you're done. Kill the heat.

**17. Serve over rice — rice stays out of the wok.**
Rice in a bowl, stir-fry spooned over the top. Do not stir the rice into the wok; it goes soggy and you lose the texture that makes the dish.

#### Nutrition *(estimated)*

| | Calories | Fat | Protein | Carbs | Fiber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whole dish** | ~4,500 | 350 g | 190 g | 105 g | 10 g |

**What a serving is:** about 1 cup of stir-fry. Served over rice as written, add roughly 200 cal and 45 g carbs per cup of jasmine rice.

*Rice is served separately and is **not** included above. Pork belly is what drives the fat number.*

**🔁 Unchanged by the 2026-09-12 sous vide revision, deliberately — and here is the honest reason.** Nothing that reaches the plate is different: the same belly, the same chicken, the same vegetables, the same sauces. The bag adds only salt, garlic powder and pepper, which is rounding error. **The one figure that genuinely moves is fat, and it moves in a direction this cookbook cannot size confidently.** A boil leaves rendered fat in the pot; a 36-hour bath leaves it in the bag; a hard wok sear then renders more of it into the wok, where some of it *does* end up on the plate with the sauce. Those pull against each other, and **no honest number can be put on the net effect without weighing the bag**, so the figure above stands rather than a made-up one replacing it. **Treat 58 g per serving as the ceiling** — every one of these paths removes fat from the meat, none adds any. *(Flagged in Open Questions per [CLAUDE.md §3b](../../CLAUDE.md).)*

### D. Variation — Geoff's Original Simmer

**Geoff's own method for the pork belly, exactly as he gave it over the phone — kept in full.** It was the body of this entry until Cody's 2026-09-12 revision moved the sous vide up front, and nothing has been removed from it. **It is also the fallback**: when there isn't a day and a half of lead time, this is how the belly gets softened, and it is what the dish was built on.

**Simmer the pork belly. Set a timer for 45–60 minutes.**
Put the pork belly in a pot whole — no need to cut it up first — cover with water, bring it to a boil, then drop it to a simmer. This is the step that keeps it from being tough; it breaks the meat down before it ever hits the wok. Geoff cut his simmer time down from what the video he learned it from called for, because it was going too soft — so lean toward 45 minutes on your first try and adjust from there. **Do not do this to the chicken** — chicken will fall apart on you.

**Running the dish this way.** The simmer is unattended, so do all the chopping while it goes — that's the hour it buys you. Then pick the body up at **Step 5** and run it straight through, except that **Steps 7 and 12 collapse back into one**: the simmered belly and the raw chicken go into the wok together for the 5–7 minutes of Step 8, the way Geoff wrote it, because a simmered belly is not a fully cooked, collagen-spent one and it will take the tossing. **There are no sear marks on this version** — that is what Cody was after and what the bath buys.

**Watch both ditches on this one, because they are close together.** Geoff's warning is that the belly goes **too soft** past about an hour — that is why he cut the time down from the video. Cody's finding is the other side of it: at the long end it comes out tasting **boiled**. And under 45 minutes it stays **chewy**, which is the problem the simmer exists to fix. Forty-five minutes is the number to start on, and taste it.

**🟡 Medium** · **Prep ~25 min** · **Cook ~1 hr 10 min** · **Start to finish ~1 hr 20 min** *(45–60 min of the cook is an unattended pork simmer — do all the chopping then)* — *the badge this entry carried until 2026-09-12, kept here with the method it describes.*

### E. Open Questions

- **⚠️ Does the split-and-reunite sequence taste right? Ask after the first cook this way.** Steps 7, 8 and 12 — belly seared alone and pulled, chicken cooked on its own, belly returned with the sauce — are **the cookbook's reasoning, not Geoff's and not Cody's.** Cody never addressed what happens to Geoff's combined 5–7 minute browning step once the belly arrives pre-cooked; the sequence written here is ordinary wok practice applied to that problem. He said *"let's just see what it tastes like,"* so this entry is asking for the verdict: **did the belly hold its cubes and its sear, and did returning it with the sauce give it enough time to take the glaze?** His answer replaces the reasoning.
- **Is 155°F for 36 hours actually soft enough?** That is the whole test of the revision. The pick and its reasoning are in the Step 2 callout — it is the longest of the three published options and therefore the most collagen conversion — but **the target is a texture, not a number**, and only he can say whether it hit it. If it still eats chewy, the lever is more time, not more heat. If it eats shreddy and won't hold a cube, come down in time.
- **How long a chill does he actually give it?** The entry says ice bath 20–30 minutes then the fridge, overnight preferred and 4 hours as a floor, reasoned from [§1](1-codys-pho.md) and [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md). What he does in practice may be shorter or may be an ice chest like §6.10's.
- **How many seconds is the belly sear, really?** Step 7 uses 2–3 minutes mostly undisturbed as a working figure and says to go by color. A wok on a home burner and a wok on a jet burner are not the same fire; his own number would be better.
- **Does the fat number move?** The Nutrition block is unchanged and says plainly why — the boil, the bag and the wok sear all pull fat in different directions and the net cannot be sized without weighing the bag. **If he ever weighs the rendered fat out of a bag, that closes it.**
- **Does Geoff know?** The simmer is his, and this entry now runs a different method in front of it. Worth telling him, and worth asking what he thinks of a sous vide belly — he may have an opinion, and it would be a source.
